Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She had also been detained during last weekend's crackdown.
Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.
By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked exam papers. A march towards parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister.
The CJP has since turned its attention to India's electoral system, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sweeping revision of voter lists known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
Critics say the exercise risks removing legitimate voters from the rolls, potentially depriving them of the right to vote. The Election Commission says it is targeting ineligible, dead and duplicate voters and denies allegations that it is favouring the ruling BJP.
Last weekend, authorities imposed severe restrictions to stop CJP supporters from reaching a planned rally, sealing off roads, shutting metro stations and deploying thousands of security personnel across Delhi.
The BBC witnessed, external dozens of protesters being detained across the capital, including students and journalists.
The action drew criticism but police defended it as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were released the following day after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. But the dispute over where they could protest was only beginning.
Police removed Jantar Mantar from Delhi's list of approved protest sites, naming three alternative venues.
Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory stands close to Parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused authorities of trying to push demonstrations away from the seat of power.
On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned to the restricted site with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar.
Police said some protesters had climbed over a locked gate and that the organisers had breached the conditions of their release. The following day, the two men were sent to jail for five days.
The arrests did little to deter the movement from announcing another demonstration.
In a video message on Thursday, Dipke urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities. He also acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again.
"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said.
By Friday morning, police had served him with a notice warning against holding the march without permission.
Authorities closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons", and offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location.
The CJP came up with a different plan. Supporters were told to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave.
"Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the movement declared in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour. It urged supporters to share their photographs online.
Opposition parties have also been holding protests against Kumar and the Election Commission.
Last week, Rahul Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were detained while attempting to march to the commission's headquarters. They have also taken their concerns to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.
Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP leaders and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to protesters, although the opposition and the youth-led movement have largely demonstrated separately.
Home Minister Amit Shah has accused the opposition of spreading falsehoods about the voter-list revision and defended the commission's independence.
For the CJP, the immediate question is how long it can sustain its protests with its three main leaders in custody.
Pasricha said the party had a team and a plan in place. "If the top three continue to stay behind bars, we will continue to protest peacefully," she said.

title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
content_c:
Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
- Published
Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external.
In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.
It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.
Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".
In a statement, the party said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."
It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.
Reform MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.
"I don't accept this happens any more in Reform than in any other party," he added.
The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."
Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.
Jenrick said he believed the undercover reporters had wanted to find evidence of party leader Nigel Farage "acting in an inappropriate way" but had not succeeded.
Two years ago, Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.
However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.
Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".
- Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Reform councillor calls TV report 'vote interference' 
  - Published12 hours ago
ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists.
He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process.
After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts.
"Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds.
Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform.
Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply."
Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt.
He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons.
In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson.
However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party.
"On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying.
"I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything.
"And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay."
He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council.
The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News.
Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place.
ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down.
In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry.
In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow."
In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go".
After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation", following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service.
Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party.
He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government.
"They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people."
In the report, Reform UK MP Sarah Pochin is filmed telling the undercover reporter that the party needed "women press officers".
"They are so chauvinistic... They just exclude you if you are a woman. There's a bit of a male issue going on."
Asked about her comments, Jenrick said Pochin was a "valued colleague" but added: "It is not my experience that the party has problems of that kind."
Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK.
"Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.
"Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Reform "need to sort these issues out".
She added: "Every party will have people who make mistakes and have bad apples, the difference is how you deal with it."

title: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears
content_c:
Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.
The Queensland coroner’s court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.
The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.
Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.
Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.
But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.
The department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole care over the objections of specialist doctors who treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).
The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.
The officer gave evidence on Friday.
“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.
“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.
“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”
She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.
But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.
Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.
The case worker agreed that she may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.
“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.
She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.
Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.
On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.
“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.
“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.
On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.
The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.
All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he would leave her.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

title: Femicide in Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence
content_c:
Femicide in Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence
October 16, 2026
The life of Maryam Yarmohammadi came to a violent end in the early hours of October 5, when the 28-year-old mother of two was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her genitalia were mutilated. She died shortly afterward in hospital. Both her husband and brother were arrested.
Media reported that about 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests. They reportedly believed that death had been the "least severe punishment" Maryam Yarmohammadi deserved.
What the young woman's relatives considered her guilty of has not been publicly reported. Yet both the circumstances of the case and the extreme violence involved follow a familiar pattern seen in so-called honor killings.
In such cases, the underlying belief is often that a man must erase a perceived "dishonor" brought upon the family by a sister, daughter or wife. Failure to do so may expose him to rejection, humiliation or social exclusion within his community.
No opportunity to defend themselves
What constitutes "honor" or "proper conduct" is often defined by family expectations or social and cultural norms. In some traditionally conservative regions, even laughing loudly or engaging in a friendly conversation with an unrelated man may be viewed as a violation of these norms.
Women accused of such transgressions are frequently denied any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves against the allegations.
For years, women's rights activists in Iran have sought to establish nationwide support networks offering counseling and protection to women at risk. One such initiative is the Campaign to End Honor Killings.
Rezvan Moghaddam, a spokesperson for the campaign, told DW that there appeared to be no activist or local group in the region capable of supporting Maryam Yarmohammadi.
Through civil society networks, the campaign has in some cases succeeded in relocating threatened women to safe locations and securing shelter for them.
Moghaddam said that Maryam Yarmohammadi's death should not be interpreted as criticism of women's rights activists in those regions: "I myself come from Khuzestan in southern Iran and am fully aware of the restrictions that exist there."
Failure of the justice system
Based on interpretations of Shariah, or Islamic law, Iran's laws do not treat women as equal citizens in many areas of life. Their ability to make decisions about education, employment or travel may depend on the consent of their fathers or, later, their husbands.
Even after a woman's death, male relatives can, under certain legal provisions, influence the course of criminal proceedings.
Iranian criminal law applies the principle of retribution in certain offenses, including murder. In homicide cases, the victim's relatives may choose either to demand retribution, which can result in the death penalty, or to pardon the perpetrator.
These provisions raise particular concerns in cases of so-called honor killings. When an alleged perpetrator is also among the relatives empowered to influence decisions on punishment or forgiveness, a serious conflict of interest emerges.
Such situations expose the protection gaps critics say exist within Iran's justice system regarding violence against women.
According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, honor killings — defined as the murder of a woman by male relatives such as her father, brother or uncle for allegedly violating social norms of modesty and family honor — accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provinces in western and southern Iran.
In March 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran reported that at least 179 women were murdered by men within their family circles in 2024. These cases were recorded as femicides.
Socially legitimized violence
It was the brutality of Maryam Yarmohammadi's murder that shocked Iranians. The murder triggered a wave of grief and outrage on social media. Many women reacted strongly to what they saw as a femicide driven by hatred in the name of "honor" and "shame."
At the same time, numerous comments focused on victim-blaming, or holding Maryam Yarmohammadi responsible for her own death. Others described the killing as the "punishment of an unfaithful woman" or attempted to justify it by "understanding the men's anger."
Men have been socialized to believe they are responsible for controlling women and monitoring their behavior and decisions, the psychoanalyst Saba Alaleh said. Male identity, she said, is tied to a woman's "obedience."
Violence becomes normalized when beliefs, social approval and silence reinforce one another within this structure, Alaleh said.
"When cultural, social, political, economic, legal and educational factors are closely intertwined, they acquire enormous power," she said. "Under such conditions, women are also highly economically dependent and lack sufficient social support. Preventive mechanisms are absent, as well. All of this increases the risk of violence."
Struggle for self-determination
Atefeh Rangriz, a sociologist and women's rights activist, told DW: "Femicides have always existed, and their political manifestations can be traced throughout history, from forced unveiling [under Reza Shah Pahlavi in the 1930s] to the slogan 'Either the headscarf or blows to the head' in the Islamic Republic."
Rangriz said women understood the path toward liberation and, despite tremendous obstacles, had achieved significant progress over the past decades.
Women in Iran have been driving since 1940. They have been allowed to vote and run for political office since 1963. Women account for half of all university graduates in the country. The number of women filing for divorce or mutually ending unhappy marriages has also continued to rise.
The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which emerged from the nationwide protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody in 2022, has further transformed public perceptions of women in Iran.
"Women have learned to focus on the present rather than postponing justice to the future. They demand it now," Rangriz said. "They want to exercise autonomy over their own bodies, live as they choose, and free themselves from the structures of domination, oppression and exploitation. It is a kind of radical revolution."
Many Iranian women no longer wear the mandatory hijab in public, openly defying the Islamic Republic's dress regulations.
Yet it remains unknown what the young mother Maryam Yarmohammadi wanted, or how she wished to live. She was brutally killed.
If you or someone you know have experienced gender-based violence, the website lila.help lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world.
This article was originally written in German.
description: The murder of a young mother has once again sparked debate in Iran over so-called honor killings, the social acceptance of violence against women and the lack of protection for people vulnerable to gender-based violence.

The life of Maryam Yarmohammadi came to a violent end in the early hours of October 5, when the 28-year-old mother of two was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her genitalia were mutilated. She died shortly afterward in hospital. Both her husband and brother were arrested.
Media reported that about 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests. They reportedly believed that death had been the "least severe punishment" Maryam Yarmohammadi deserved.
What the young woman's relatives considered her guilty of has not been publicly reported. Yet both the circumstances of the case and the extreme violence involved follow a familiar pattern seen in so-called honor killings.
In such cases, the underlying belief is often that a man must erase a perceived "dishonor" brought upon the family by a sister, daughter or wife. Failure to do so may expose him to rejection, humiliation or social exclusion within his community.
No opportunity to defend themselves
What constitutes "honor" or "proper conduct" is often defined by family expectations or social and cultural norms. In some traditionally conservative regions, even laughing loudly or engaging in a friendly conversation with an unrelated man may be viewed as a violation of these norms.
Women accused of such transgressions are frequently denied any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves against the allegations.
For years, women's rights activists in Iran have sought to establish nationwide support networks offering counseling and protection to women at risk. One such initiative is the Campaign to End Honor Killings.
Rezvan Moghaddam, a spokesperson for the campaign, told DW that there appeared to be no activist or local group in the region capable of supporting Maryam Yarmohammadi.
Through civil society networks, the campaign has in some cases succeeded in relocating threatened women to safe locations and securing shelter for them.
Moghaddam said that Maryam Yarmohammadi's death should not be interpreted as criticism of women's rights activists in those regions: "I myself come from Khuzestan in southern Iran and am fully aware of the restrictions that exist there."
Failure of the justice system
Based on interpretations of Shariah, or Islamic law, Iran's laws do not treat women as equal citizens in many areas of life. Their ability to make decisions about education, employment or travel may depend on the consent of their fathers or, later, their husbands.
Even after a woman's death, male relatives can, under certain legal provisions, influence the course of criminal proceedings.
Iranian criminal law applies the principle of retribution in certain offenses, including murder. In homicide cases, the victim's relatives may choose either to demand retribution, which can result in the death penalty, or to pardon the perpetrator.
These provisions raise particular concerns in cases of so-called honor killings. When an alleged perpetrator is also among the relatives empowered to influence decisions on punishment or forgiveness, a serious conflict of interest emerges.
Such situations expose the protection gaps critics say exist within Iran's justice system regarding violence against women.
According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, honor killings — defined as the murder of a woman by male relatives such as her father, brother or uncle for allegedly violating social norms of modesty and family honor — accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provinces in western and southern Iran.
In March 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran reported that at least 179 women were murdered by men within their family circles in 2024. These cases were recorded as femicides.
Socially legitimized violence
It was the brutality of Maryam Yarmohammadi's murder that shocked Iranians. The murder triggered a wave of grief and outrage on social media. Many women reacted strongly to what they saw as a femicide driven by hatred in the name of "honor" and "shame."
At the same time, numerous comments focused on victim-blaming, or holding Maryam Yarmohammadi responsible for her own death. Others described the killing as the "punishment of an unfaithful woman" or attempted to justify it by "understanding the men's anger."
Men have been socialized to believe they are responsible for controlling women and monitoring their behavior and decisions, the psychoanalyst Saba Alaleh said. Male identity, she said, is tied to a woman's "obedience."
Violence becomes normalized when beliefs, social approval and silence reinforce one another within this structure, Alaleh said.
"When cultural, social, political, economic, legal and educational factors are closely intertwined, they acquire enormous power," she said. "Under such conditions, women are also highly economically dependent and lack sufficient social support. Preventive mechanisms are absent, as well. All of this increases the risk of violence."
Struggle for self-determination
Atefeh Rangriz, a sociologist and women's rights activist, told DW: "Femicides have always existed, and their political manifestations can be traced throughout history, from forced unveiling [under Reza Shah Pahlavi in the 1930s] to the slogan 'Either the headscarf or blows to the head' in the Islamic Republic."
Rangriz said women understood the path toward liberation and, despite tremendous obstacles, had achieved significant progress over the past decades.
Women in Iran have been driving since 1940. They have been allowed to vote and run for political office since 1963. Women account for half of all university graduates in the country. The number of women filing for divorce or mutually ending unhappy marriages has also continued to rise.
The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which emerged from the nationwide protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody in 2022, has further transformed public perceptions of women in Iran.
"Women have learned to focus on the present rather than postponing justice to the future. They demand it now," Rangriz said. "They want to exercise autonomy over their own bodies, live as they choose, and free themselves from the structures of domination, oppression and exploitation. It is a kind of radical revolution."
Many Iranian women no longer wear the mandatory hijab in public, openly defying the Islamic Republic's dress regulations.
Yet it remains unknown what the young mother Maryam Yarmohammadi wanted, or how she wished to live. She was brutally killed.
If you or someone you know have experienced gender-based violence, the website lila.help lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world.
This article was originally written in German.

title: »Rente mit 63«: Arbeitsminister Alexander Schweitzer plädiert für Kompromiss
content_c:
Reform der Alterssicherung Arbeitsminister Schweitzer plädiert für Kompromiss zu »Rente mit 63«
Der neue Bundesarbeitsminister Alexander Schweitzer strebt im Streit über die abschlagsfreie Frührente nach 45 Beitragsjahren einen »guten Kompromiss« an. »Ich bin zuversichtlich, dass uns das gelingen wird«, sagte der SPD-Politiker der »Rheinpfalz«. Die Vorschläge der Rentenkommission sehen vor, die sogenannte Rente mit 63 abzuschaffen. Schweitzer, der am Mittwoch als Minister vereidigt wurde, hatte sich im August gegen die Abschaffung ausgesprochen .
Er betonte nun, dass Schwarz-Rot sich im Koalitionsvertrag darauf geeinigt habe, die abschlagsfreie Rente nach 45 Beitragsjahren grundsätzlich beizubehalten. Jetzt habe die Alterssicherungskommission »einen Vorschlag gemacht, der davon abweicht«. Das kritisierten auch manche CDU-Ministerpräsidenten, hob Schweitzer hervor. »Deshalb wird das genau eines der Themen sein, bei denen wir uns zusammensetzen und einen guten Kompromiss finden müssen.«
Widerstand bei SPD und CDU
Die von der Bundesregierung eingesetzte Rentenkommission hatte im Juni 33 Vorschläge für eine umfassende Rentenreform vorgelegt, darunter die Abschaffung der abschlagsfreien Rente nach 45 Versicherungsjahren. Kanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) und die am Montag zurückgetretene Arbeitsministerin Bärbel Bas (SPD) hatten damals angekündigt, die Vorschläge vollständig umzusetzen.
Gegen die Abschaffung der abschlagsfreien Frührente gibt es schon länger Widerstand in der SPD. Allerdings hatten sich auch die drei ostdeutschen CDU-Ministerpräsidenten Sven Schulze (Sachsen-Anhalt), Michael Kretschmer (Sachsen) und Mario Voigt (Thüringen) gegen die Pläne gestellt .
Vorschläge statt «Gesamtkunstwerk»
Angesprochen auf die Aussage seiner Vorgängerin Bärbel Bas, die Rentenvorschläge seien ein Gesamtkunstwerk, sagte Schweitzer: »Kommissionsvorschläge sind Kommissionsvorschläge sind Kommissionsvorschläge.« Auf ihrer Grundlage »dürfen und müssen politische Debatten stattfinden«, hob der Minister hervor. »Die Entscheidungen werden in der Regierung und im Bundestag gefällt, so gehört sich das in einer parlamentarischen Demokratie.«
description: Ex-Ministerin Bärbel Bas nannte die Rentenreform ein »Gesamtkunstwerk«. Ihr Nachfolger Alexander Schweitzer fordert nun eine neue Debatte über die abschlagsfreie Rente und beruft sich dabei auf einen wichtigen Vertrag.

title: Selenskyj beim EU-Gipfel: Unterstützung für die Ukraine ohne USA?
content_c:
Selenskyj beim EU-Gipfel Kann Europa die Ukraine allein unterstützen?
Die Gräben zwischen den USA und der Ukraine scheinen immer größer zu werden. Selenskyj wendet sich mit einer Grundsatzfrage an die EU-Staaten - die haben militärische, finanzielle und politische Probleme.
Über eine Stunde lässt der ukrainische Präsident Selenskyj den voll besetzten Presseraum im Justus-Lipsius-Gebäude warten. Es habe noch Gesprächsbedarf mit den europäischen Staats- und Regierungschefs gegeben, sagt sein Pressesprecher zur Entschuldigung, als es endlich losgeht.
Wer Selenskyj danach richtig zuhört, der versteht sofort, worin der große Gesprächsbedarf bestanden hat. Selenskyj macht heute eine grundsätzliche Frage auf, die die EU, so gut es geht, seit Jahren vermeidet: Kann die Europäische Union die Ukraine allein unterstützen - militärisch, finanziell, politisch?
USA wenden sich Russland zu
Denn: Die Verwerfungen zwischen Washington und Kiew sind im Moment riesig, die USA drohen jetzt vollständig, als Unterstützer der Ukraine auszufallen - sie wenden sich im Gegenteil Moskau zu. Präsident Donald Trump hat Sanktionen gegen Russland ausgesetzt, um billigen Treibstoff zu bekommen. Er kritisiert die Ukraine für ihre Taktik, Russlands Raffinerien und Pipelines anzugreifen - und das Weiße Haus hat anscheinend zumindest teilweise die technische Unterstützung für die Ukraine eingestellt.
Das Abschalten des militärischen Teils der amerikanischen Starlink-Satelliten ist nicht einfach ein Versehen, es trifft Kiew an einem empfindlichen Punkt: Ohne diese Augen im All ist die Vorwarnzeit bei russischen Angriffen sehr kurz, ukrainische Abfangdrohnen funktionieren ohne Starlink nur ungenügend, die Einschläge auch in der ukrainischen Hauptstadt nehmen zu.
"Die wahren Führer der freien Welt"
Selenskyj verbindet seine kritischen Aussagen zu Washington heute immer mit einer demonstrativen Hinwendung an die EU: Die Europäer seien die verlässlichen Verbündeten der Ukraine. Schon am Morgen nennt er ihre Staats- und Regierungschefs die "wahren Führer der freien Welt". Es gibt nicht wenige hier, die das sehr gern hören.
Der ukrainische Präsident zeigt aber auch sofort die Konsequenzen auf: Wenn die USA jetzt droht, als Verbündeter vollständig auszufallen, muss Europa handeln, soll der Krieg nicht verloren gehen. Die Forderungen sind ganz konkret: Man habe "Patriot"-Batterien zur Verteidigung der großen ukrainischen Städte stationiert, dafür brauche es jetzt die PAC2- und PAC3-Raketen, die die US-Amerikaner gerade in großen Mengen am Persischen Golf verbrauchen.
Unterstützung mit allem, was die Ukraine braucht
Die Europäer hätten genug solcher Raketen auf Lager, um die Ukraine durch den Winter zu bringen, sagt Selenskyj - sie sollten sie also bitte liefern. Natürlich kennt auch er die Vorbehalte vieler EU-Staaten, die Depots ausgerechnet jetzt zu leeren. Aber, so sagt er auf Nachfrage, es sei eine einfache Entscheidung - wenn die Aussage wirklich stimme, dass Europa die Ukraine mit allem unterstützen wolle, was sie brauche.
Deutschland hat eine Lizenz zum Nachbau der US-amerikanischen Raketen erhalten - auch wenn es nur für die ältere Version ist. Aber es wird noch etwa ein Jahr dauern, bis die Produktion anläuft. Für den Winter wird das noch keine Hilfe sein.
90 Milliarden Euro fast aufgebraucht
Und dann braucht die Ukraine mehr Geld, auch das trifft die Europäer an einem sensiblen Punkt: Vor einem Jahr hat man mit viel Mühe und unter politischen Verrenkungen einen 90-Milliarden-Euro-Unterstützungspakt zusammengezimmert, der aber sollte "für absehbare Zeit" genügen, wie der Ratspräsident vor einem Jahr formulierte. Diese Zeit scheint schon vorbei zu sein.
Manche ukrainischen Quellen sprechen nun davon, dass ein Fehlbetrag von 70 Milliarden Euro ausgeglichen werden müsse. Viele Regierungschefs zweifeln diese Summe an, beinahe ungläubig darüber, dass anscheinend 90 Milliarden Euro fast aufgebraucht sind.
Man hat jetzt erst einmal die Ukraine zu einem Kassensturz aufgefordert, Kiew solle die exakte Summe nennen. Aber wenn sich der Fehlbetrag wirklich in dieser Höhe bewegt, könnte es für die Staats- und Regierungschefs eng werden.
Gemeinsame Schulden absolutes No-Go
Wieder wird die Frage aufkommen, ob man die eingefrorenen russischen Vermögen, die in Belgien liegen, für solche Zahlungen nutzen kann, wieder wird die belgische Regierung sich mit Händen und Füßen dagegen wehren. Das letzte Mal hatte sie damit überraschenderweise Erfolg.
Die Alternative aber, eine gemeinsame Schuldenaufnahme aller EU-Staaten, ist für Geberstaaten wie Deutschland der Gottseibeiuns der Finanzdebatten - ein absolutes No-Go. Außerdem kommt die Debatte ausgerechnet zu einer Zeit, in der man einen billionenschweren EU-Haushalt für die kommenden sieben Jahre vereinbaren will, den die meisten Rechtsaußenparteien in Europa als verantwortungslose Geldverschwendung geißeln.
EU-Beitrittskandidaten stehen Schlange
Wenn die EU wirklich die USA ersetzen soll, wäre vermutlich auch ein zeitnaher EU-Beitritt der Ukraine sinnvoll. Aber auch wenn die EU-Spitze vor laufenden Kameras heute verkündet, dass man noch einmal zwei Verhandlungskapitel mit Kiew eröffnen werde, so wissen alle - auch der ukrainische Präsident -, dass sich die Ukraine mit ihrer riesigen Fläche, ihrer großen Landwirtschaft und ihren Problemen mit korrupten Strukturen in der Schlange der Beitrittskandidaten hinten anstellen müssen wird.
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz sagt heute, dass Moldau und Montenegro eigentlich wesentlich mehr Fortschritte gemacht hätten und dass man eben nach solchen Fortschritten entscheiden müsse. Das mag nachvollziehbar sein, politisch wird das allerdings heikel und schwer vermittelbar, der Protest der baltischen Staaten gegen eine solche Haltung ("keine Erweiterung ohne die Ukraine") gibt schon jetzt einen schwachen Vorgeschmack.
Resthoffnung in die USA
Selenskyj also stellt heute genau diese drei Fragen an die EU: Wie weit können die EU-Staaten der Ukraine militärisch, finanziell und politisch helfen? Die Antwort fällt in jedem dieser Punkte verhalten aus. Und: Noch gibt es anscheinend eine Resthoffnung, die USA von ihrem Pro-Russland-Kurs wieder abzubringen. Noch schrecken alle davor zurück, die USA zu heftig zu kritisieren, auch der ukrainische Präsident.
Am Ende der Pressekonferenz wird Selenskyj gefragt, ob er glaube, dass jetzt er und die Ukraine für Donald Trumps verfehlte Politik büßen müssten. Er blickt zu Boden, dann schaut er auf und grinst in die Kamera und sagt: "Das ist meine Antwort."

title: Was Sie über "hirnfressende" Amöben wissen sollten
content_c:
Was Sie über "hirnfressende" Amöben wissen sollten
Veröffentlicht 4. August 2023Zuletzt aktualisiert 16. Oktober 2026
Eine Infektion mit der Amöbe Naegleria fowleri ist selten, allerdings verläuft die Infektion fast immer tödlich. Deshalb haben die Behörden des mexikanischen Bundesstaates Yucatán sechs Seen gesperrt, in denen der Parasit nachgewiesen werden konnte. Ein 34-jähriger Mann, der als Wasserskilehrer gearbeitet hatte, war im September an einer durch Neagleria fowleri verursachten Hirnentzündung gestorben.
Auch in den USA sterben immer wieder Menschen durch die Amöbe. Laut der amerikanischen Gesundheitsbehörde CDC erkranken jährlich zwar weniger als zehn Menschen an der sogenannten Primären Amöben-Meningoenzephalitis (PAM), allerdings sind die Folgen einer Infektion fatal: 97 Prozent der Erkrankten sterben.
Wo gibt es "hirnfressende" Amöben?
Naegleria fowleri ist thermophil, das heißt, die Amöbe mag warme Süßwasser und Böden am liebsten. Sie ist deshalb vor allem in den Subtropen und Tropen verbreitet, findet sich laut Robert-Koch-Institut (RKI) in den Sommermonaten aber auch in natürlich oder künstlich erwärmten Gewässern in gemäßigten Klimazonen. Laut CDC vermehrt sich Naegleria fowleri ab einer Temperatur von etwa 30 Grad Celsius bis hin zu 46 Grad Celsius am besten.
In seltenen Fällen gedeihen die einzelligen Lebewesen auch in nicht ausreichend gechlorten Pools oder verunreinigtem Trinkwasser. In Salzwasser hingegen kommt Naegleria fowleri nicht vor.
Was passiert bei einer Infektion mit Naegleria fowleri?
Normalerweise ernähren sich Amöben von Bakterien, die sie im Wasser und Boden entdecken. Manchmal findet die Amöbe allerdings ihren Weg über die Nase einer Person in den menschlichen Körper. Das kann beim Schwimmen, Tauchen oder auch beim Reinigen der Nase mit kontaminiertem Wasser passieren. Von dort dringt Naegleri fowleri über den ersten Hirnnerv (Nervus olfactorius), der für den Geruchssinn zuständig ist, bis ins Gehirn vor.
Die Inkubationszeit, also die Zeit von der Infektion bis zum Ausbruch der Erkrankung, beträgt zwischen drei und bis zu 14 Tagen. Die Infizierten bekommen Fieber, leiden unter Übelkeit, Erbrechen und Kopfschmerzen. Wahrnehmungs- und Bewegungsstörungen folgen. Es kommt zu einer sogenannten hämorrhagisch nekrotisierenden Meningoenzephalitis, einer Entzündung des Gehirns, die das Hirngewebe zerstört. Die Betroffenen fallen ins Koma und sterben in den meisten Fällen.
Laut CDC ist eine Infektion mit Naegleri fowleri ausschließlich über die Nase möglich. Eine Übertragung durch Tröpfchen oder Aerosole über die Luft findet nicht statt. Auch das Trinken von kontaminiertem Wasser ist ungefährlich - zumindest was eine Infektion mit der "hirnfressenden" Amöbe angeht.
Wie wird eine Infektion behandelt?
Wer nach dem Baden in einem warmen See Kopfschmerzen, einen steifen Nacken und Fieber bekommt und sich übergeben muss, sollte sich schnellstmöglich in ärztliche Behandlung begeben.
Die Primäre Amöben-Meningoenzephalitis (PAM) wird mit einer Kombination von Medikamenten behandelt - darunter Antibiotika wie Rifampin und Antimykotika wie Amphotericin B, die für die Behandlung von Pilzinfektionen entwickelt wurden. Diese Medikamente wurden bereits erfolgreich zur Behandlung von Patienten eingesetzt, die überlebt haben. Miltefosin, ursprünglich zur Therapie von Brustkrebs angewendet, ist das neueste Medikament, das sich im Einsatz gegen die Amöbe vielversprechend zeigt.
Da die PAM so selten ist und die Erkrankung, einmal ausgebrochen, so rasant abläuft, gestaltet sich die Suche nach effizienten Therapien schwierig.
Die Klimakrise könnte das Problem verschärfen, weil sich mit steigenden Luft- auch die Wassertemperaturen erhöhen. Laut CDC infizieren sich mittlerweile nicht mehr nur Menschen in den südlichen US-Bundesstaaten, auch aus dem Norden der USA werden Erkrankungen gemeldet.

title: Київ розігріє до +17 °C, але є нюанс: якою буде погода у столиці та області 17 жовтня
content_c:
Київ розігріє до +17 °C, але є нюанс: якою буде погода у столиці та області 17 жовтня
Осіннє похолодання та дощі у столичному регіоні затримаються ненадовго, адже синоптики вже прогнозують підвищення температури наступного тижня.
У суботу, 17 жовтня, у Києві та на Київщині утримуватиметься хмарна погода з можливими невеликими дощами.
Синоптикиня Наталка Діденко прогнозує у столиці 17 жовтня погоду без опадів та з температурою повітря від +15 до +17 градусів вище нуля. В неділю очікуються дощі.
«На наступному тижні, орієнтовно із вівторка-середи, синоптична ситуація в Україні вирівняється, атмосферний тиск підросте, дощі припиняться, а температура повітря підвищиться», — повідомляє Діденко.
В Українському гідрометцентрі повідомляють, що 17 жовтня по території Київщини та міста Києва буде хмарно та очікуються невеликі дощі. Вітер дутиме східний та зі швидкістю 5-10 м/с.
Температура повітря по області вдень становитиме від +13 до +18 градусів тепла, у столиці повітря прогріється до +14…+16 градусів вище нуля.
На погодному порталі Sinoptik прогнозують у столиці 17 жовтня хмарну погоду. Протягом усього дня очікується дрібний дощ. Температура повітря у денні години становитиме від +11 до +14 градусів вище нуля.
Раніше синоптики розповіли, якою буде погода в Україні 17 жовтня.
Підписуйтесь на наші канали у Telegram та Viber.

title: Очереди до 40 часов: на границе с Польшей задерживаются грузовики
content_c:
В связи с объявлением воздушной тревоги в регионах Украины, расположенных вблизи польской границы, на пунктах пропуска с Польшей приостановили оформление грузовиков и автобусов. Из-за этого время ожидания на некоторых пунктах пропуска достигло 40 часов. Об этом сообщил представитель Люблинской налоговой администрации Михал Дерусь, передает Polskie Radio.
По его словам, только в течение нескольких часов ночью 16 октября воздушная тревога объявлялась девять раз, а ещё несколько раз — утром.
«В Дорогуске таможенного оформления приходится ждать 40 часов, в Гребенном — более 24 часов, а в Зосине — восемь часов», — сказал Дерусь.
Также в Гребенном оформления ожидают 880 грузовиков, а в Зосине — 250.
Всего за прошедшие сутки сотрудники таможенной и налоговой служб на пограничных переходах в Люблинском воеводстве оформили и пропустили более 3 тысяч грузовиков и более 3,7 тысячи легковых автомобилей.
В то же время в Государственной пограничной службе Украины (ГПСУ) не комментировали заявления польской стороны.
В Минразвития ранее сообщали, что Украина рассматривает возможность переноса пунктов пропуска на территорию соседних государств из-за систематических российских атак. После инцидентов с российскими беспилотниками Польша привлекла военных к охране шести пунктов пропуска на границе с Украиной.

title: Унаслідок авіаудару по Херсону загинув водій "швидкої", поранено чотирьох людей, зокрема немовля та дитину – МВА
content_c:
Російські окупаційні війська в суботу вранці завдали авіаудару по Корабельному району Херсона, унаслідок чого загинув водій екстреної медичної допомоги та постраждали четверо цивільних, серед яких двоє дітей, повідомив начальник Херсонської міської військової адміністрації Ярослав Шанько.
"Внаслідок ранкового авіаудару по Корабельному району Херсона загинула людина. Черговою жертвою російських терористів став 64-річний чоловік – водій екстреної медичної допомоги. Він отримав травми, несумісні з життям", – зазначив очільник МВА в телеграм-каналі.
За його даними, серед чотирьох поранених – родина з одномісячним немовлям та 11-річна дівчинка. Дитина зазнала вибухової й закритої черепно-мозкової травм, акубаротравми та забою потилиці, її стан оцінюють як середньої тяжкості.
У власній квартирі під час атаки постраждали троє членів сім'ї: 28-річна жінка, 37-річний чоловік та їхня одномісячна дитина. Усі вони зазнали вибухових, закритих черепно-мозкових травм і контузій та були госпіталізовані в стані середнього ступеня тяжкості.

title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
content_c:
Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
- Published
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.
"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."
Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
His failure to establish that the window was not closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.
"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences," he said.
The judge added there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.
She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk.
After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".
He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.
He described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
His failure to establish that the window was not closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.
"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences," he said.
The judge added there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.
She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk.
After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".
He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.
He described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

title: 'Massive challenge' to protect Donaldson from harm in jail
content_c:
'Massive challenge' to protect Donaldson from harm in jail
- Published
Protecting convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson from harm inside jail will be a "massive risk-management headache" for prison bosses, according to a former governor.
The ex-Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader was given a 15-year sentence on Thursday after being convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including rape, against two women when they were children.
He is serving his sentence at Maghaberry Prison near Lisburn but will spend only half of his term behind bars.
Ian Acheson, who worked for HM Prison Service for about a decade, said the former Lagan Valley MP faced risks from fellow inmates.
Donaldson represents a "very complex challenge to the Northern Ireland Prison Service", Acheson added.
"There are always hierarchies within prisons - and there are even hierarchies within sex offenders - and the lowest of the low and the most vulnerable in terms of hostility from others are those who've been convicted of sexual violence against a minor," he said.
But he said it would also be necessary to "examine potential political or sectarian targeting" relating to Donaldson's leadership of the DUP and his service in the Ulster Defence Regiment, a former Army unit.
"The prison has a duty of care to protect him and he is uniquely vulnerable," Acheson told BBC Radio Ulster's Talkback programme.
"Maghaberry, in previous inspections, has indicated that it operates an integrated regime, where sex offenders can be safely managed in the wider prison community.
"I don't think that is remotely viable for Jeffrey Donaldson, given those offence characteristics and his background.
"So either he is kept, in effect, in conditions of solitary confinement for years and years or another solution has to be found.
"I don't think it's acceptable to keep him in conditions of solitary confinement - it may not even be legal."
Reading in his cell
Donaldson spends up to 18 hours a day in his cell at Maghaberry Prison, which holds about 1,600 inmates.
It is thought he has been put in the Moyola Unit, which primarily houses prisoners with health issues, for his own safety as it isolates him from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners.
He is believed to spend much of his day reading books from the prison library.
Acheson said the disgraced former politician was "entitled to protection but he's not entitled to special, preferential treatment".
There was a "precedent within the UK" to transfer prisoners within different jurisdictions, Acheson added - therefore Donaldson "could be potentially compulsorily transferred" to another jail.
Donaldson was convicted in June of sex offences against two females referred to in his trial as Victim A and Victim B.
He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A.
He will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life.
During sentencing, Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace".
Donaldson, who denied the charges, is seeking to appeal his convictions.
Should his attempt to appeal fail, he will be released from prison at the end of 2033.
He qualifies for a 50% remission in his sentence because the offences were committed before the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 came into effect.
The remainder of his sentence will be served under supervision in the community on licence.
Who is Jeffrey Donaldson?
Donaldson's time in politics began in 1985 when he was elected for the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) as a member of the Stormont assembly for South Down.
In 1997, Donaldson became the MP for Lagan Valley, representing the UUP. He would remain an MP until 2024.
However, in 2003 he quit the UUP and defected to the DUP.
Donaldson was awarded a knighthood in the 2016 Queen's Birthday Honours list, and, in 2021, became leader of the DUP.
He remained the party's leader until March 2024, when he was charged with a series of historical sexual offences against children.
After his conviction this year, Donaldson asked for his knighthood to be forfeited and tendered his resignation from the Privy Council with immediate effect.
In July, King Charles stripped Donaldson of his knighthood.

title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?
content_c:
Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.
In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).
Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.
Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.
“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”
After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”
If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.
Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.
The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe.
Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.
“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.
“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.
“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”
The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.
Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.
Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.
“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.
“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”
She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”
The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss.
France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard.
In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.
Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.
“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.
In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.
Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.
As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.
“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.
Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”
The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.
“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.
“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”

title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama
content_c:
Can Albania's student protests bring political change?
October 16, 2026
The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.
She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.
"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."
University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.
Escalation after months of protests
Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution." The protests began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.
The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.
Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.
A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.
The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down. They say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.
"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.
Rama breaks his silence
During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.
Then, at 8:03 a.m. local time on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.
"These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.
Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.
The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.
The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the EU. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.
Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.
"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.
"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," Xhemollari told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama's administration alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.
"We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
What could come after the protests?
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.
Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.
"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," Xhemollari told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama's administration alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.
"We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
What could come after the protests?
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.
Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

title: US-Neuverschuldung steigt unter Trump auf Fünf-Jahres-Hoch
content_c:
Fast zwei Billionen US-Dollar US-Neuverschuldung steigt unter Trump auf Fünf-Jahres-Hoch
Die Neuverschuldung der USA ist trotz der von Präsident Donald Trump angekündigten Ausgabenkürzungen auf den höchsten Stand seit 2021 gestiegen. Im Haushaltsjahr 2026, das Ende September endete, betrug das Defizit 1,99 Billionen Dollar und damit zwölf Prozent mehr als im Vorjahr, wie das Finanzministerium am Freitag in Washington mitteilte.
Im vorherigen Haushaltsjahr hatte das Defizit noch 1,78 Billionen Dollar betragen. Die Ausgaben der Bundesregierung in Washington stiegen nun um sechs Prozent auf 7,4 Billionen Dollar, während die Einnahmen lediglich um drei Prozent auf 5,4 Billionen Dollar zulegten.
Besonders stark belasteten steigende Schuldzinsen den Haushalt . Die Zinszahlungen erhöhten sich um 144 Milliarden Dollar auf den Rekordwert von 1,36 Billionen Dollar. Hinzu kamen Rückzahlungen von insgesamt 145 Milliarden Dollar an Zöllen, nachdem der Oberste Gerichtshof im Februar einen Großteil von Trumps Zöllen für ungültig erklärt hatte.
Durch das Defizit wächst der Schuldenberg der USA weiter deutlich an. Die gesamte Staatsverschuldung der USA hatte zuletzt erstmals die Schwelle von 40 Billionen Dollar (aktuell knapp 34,4 Billionen Euro) überschritten, wie das Finanzministerium im August mitgeteilt hatte.
Trump hatte nach seiner Rückkehr ins Weiße Haus versprochen, die Staatsausgaben und somit auch die Neuverschuldung zu senken. Finanzminister Scott Bessent hatte eine Verringerung auf drei Prozent als Ziel ausgegeben. Nach Angaben des Finanzministeriums lag das Defizit nun aber bei geschätzt 6,2 Prozent der Wirtschaftsleistung.
Wirtschaftswissenschaftlerin Nancy Vanden Houten von Oxford Economics erwartet im kommenden Haushaltsjahr ein ähnlich hohes Defizit. Sollte der Krieg mit dem Iran bis weit in das neue Haushaltsjahr andauern, könne das Haushaltsloch noch größer ausfallen, warnte sie.

title: Angriff auf NS-Dokumentationszentrum in Köln
content_c:
Köln Buttersäure-Anschlag auf NS-Dokumentationszentrum
In der Nacht auf Freitag ist das NS-Dokumentationszentrum in Köln mit einer übelriechenden Flüssigkeit verunreinigt worden. Die Polizei geht von einem Buttersäure-Angriff aus. Am Nachmittag gab es eine Mahnwache.
Am Freitagmorgen hatten Mitarbeiter der Einrichtung am Appellhofplatz infolge der extremen Geruchsbelästigung die Polizei informiert. Diese stellte fest, dass die Eingangsbereiche an allen drei Zugängen des Gebäudes mit einer übelriechenden Flüssigkeit verunreinigt wurden. Die Polizei geht von einem Buttersäure-Angriff aus. Weil die Tat einen politischen Hintergrund haben könnte, ermittelt der Staatsschutz.
Betroffenheit und Wut nach Angriff auf EL-DE-Haus
Der Angriff auf eine solche Institution sei ein Angriff auf die Erinnerungskultur, sagte Claudia Wörmann, die Co-Vorsitzende des Fördervereins des NS-Dokumentationszentrums, gegenüber dem WDR.
                
                
                Es macht mich betroffen, aber auch wütend.
Claudia Wörmann, Co-Vorsitzende des Fördervereins des NS-DOK
Denn es sei auch ein Angriff auf die heutige Arbeit des NS-DOK. Dieses leistet viel Aufklärungsarbeit gegen Rassismus, Antisemitismus und Rechtsextremismus.
Mit ihrer Empörung ist Claudia Wörmann nicht allein. Als Zeichen der Solidarität versammelten sich etwa 50 Menschen für eine spontane Kundgebung und Mahnwache vor dem Gebäude.
"Angriff auf das demokratische Selbstverständnis"
Kölns Oberbürgermeister Torsten Burmester verurteilte die Tat aufs Schärfste. "Das NS-DOK ist nicht irgendein Gebäude, sondern der Ort in Köln, an dem wir die Verbrechen des Nationalsozialismus erforschen, sichtbar machen und an die Opfer erinnern", hieß es in einer Mitteilung der Stadt. Damit sei es ein Angriff auf die Erinnerungskultur und das demokratische Selbstverständnis der Stadt.
"Ohne den polizeilichen Ermittlungen vorgreifen zu wollen, müssen wir den Vorfall als gezielten Angriff auf die Gedenkstätte und die Erinnerungskultur zum Nationalsozialismus in Köln begreifen", sagte Henning Borggräfe, der Leiter des Zentrums. Man verurteile den Angriff scharf, werde sich davon aber nicht verunsichern lassen.
Zentrum "für eine lebendige Erinnerungskultur"
Auch die Kölner Landtagsabgeordnete der Grünen, Berîvan Aymaz, meldete sich am Freitag zu Wort. "Der feige Angriff auf das NS-Dokumentationszentrum in meiner Heimatstadt Köln ist abscheulich." Gerade in Zeiten, in denen Rechtsextremismus, Antisemitismus und Rassismus erstarken, müssten solche Orte geschützt und gestärkt werden, so die Vizepräsidentin des NRW-Landtags. "Sie sind unverzichtbar für eine lebendige Erinnerungskultur und unsere demokratische Gesellschaft."
Etwa 50 Menschen versammelten sich spontan am Freitagnachmittag zu einer Mahnwache.
Erst Donnerstagabend hatte es im NS-DOK eine Podiumsdiskussion über die Einstufung der AfD durch den Verfassungsschutz gegeben. Ob ein Zusammenhang besteht, ist aber bislang unklar.
Ort der Erinnerung an den Nationalsozialismus
Wie die Stadt mitteilte, werde das Zentrum aufgrund der Reinigungsarbeiten bis einschließlich Montag geschlossen bleiben. Am Dienstag soll die Gedenkstätte dann wieder regulär öffnen.
Das NS-DOK ist ein Zentrum zur Aufarbeitung des Nationalsozialismus in Köln und Umgebung und ein Ort der Erinnerung. Es befindet sich im historischen EL-DE-Haus in der Kölner Innenstadt. Als Museum und Gedenkstätte sammelt und bewahrt es Zeugnisse zur NS-Zeit. Außerdem veranstaltet es Ausstellungen und leistet Bildungs- und Beratungsarbeit.
Unsere Quellen:
- Polizei Köln
- Stadt Köln
- Interview Claudia Wörmann
